extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and literary scholars interested in Joseph Heller's Catch-22 and absurdist/dark-comedy fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the narrative, stylistic, thematic, and structural features that define Catch-22 and similar absurdist/dark-comedy novels, and the devices by which they produce satirical and comic (yet often tragic) effects. Useful for literary analysis, teaching, or emulating the novel's techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-chronological third-person omniscient narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses a distinctive non-chronological third-person omniscient narration, describing events from the points of view of different characters; separate storylines are out of sequence so the timeline develops along with the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel's timeline is intentionally fragmented so the reader must piece events together; this structure supports both comic reveals and thematic layering. As a production guideline, avoid linear exposition and let chronology emerge from interwoven character perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirizes military bureaucracy and greed
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel satirizes military bureaucracy and greed, using characters and plot to critique institutional priorities and self-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target institutional absurdities and profit motives (e.g., officers raising mission counts for promotion) rather than only individual failings; exaggeration and ironic outcomes help make the satire effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular, repetitive prose and paradoxical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Heller's prose is circular and repetitive, exemplifying the structure of a Catch-22; circular reasoning and paradox are widely used by characters to justify actions and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and circular logic can be used deliberately to mirror the theme (no-win rules) and to generate comic irony; include examples and aphoristic paradoxes to emphasize institutional illogic. Beware of overuse that becomes mere redundancy rather than purposeful symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of events from differing points of view to complete jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many events are repeatedly described from differing points of view so the reader learns more about each event from each iteration, with new information often completing a joke whose setup appeared earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated iterations to add layers of detail and to turn earlier setups into later punchlines; this technique creates a sense of payoff across nonsequential chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-association, episodic structure that is nevertheless highly structured
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the structure may seem random, the book is founded on free association: ideas run into one another through seemingly random connections, creating episodic chapters that are linked (e.g., minor characters or incidents bridging chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design episodes that can stand alone thematically but are connected through associative links (recurrent characters, objects, or lines). Use connectors (small recurring elements) to bind episodes into an emergent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic chapter focus and extensive character development
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual chapters often deal with thematically unique ideas and many named characters are described in detail with fleshed-out or multidimensional personas, leaving few true 'minor' characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign chapters to character-focused themes; develop supporting characters fully rather than treating them as mere background to enrich the satirical tapestry. This supports varied comic angles and cumulative world-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox and no-win situations (the Catch-22 concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses paradox as a central motif: a Catch-22 is 'a problem for which the only solution is denied by a circumstance inherent in the problem or by a rule' (e.g., if one is crazy one does not have to fly missions, but applying to be excused proves sanity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct institutional rules or logical traps that produce self-contradictory outcomes; the humor and critique arise from the apparent logic that yields an absurd or cruel result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce driven by miscommunication, sometimes leading to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the farce is fueled by intentional and unintentional miscommunication, occasionally leading to tragic consequences (e.g., sabotaged correspondence, mis-censoring of letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit misunderstandings and bureaucratic bungling for comic effect while allowing some comic situations to escalate into serious harm to underscore the tragedy beneath the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theodicy and existential questioning as tonal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel explores theodicy—questioning a benevolent, competent God—and uses existential questioning to deepen the tragicomic tone (e.g., Yossarian's reflections on pain, incompetence, and suffering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave philosophical questioning into comedic scenes to produce dark humor and to complicate simple satirical targets; use rhetorical lament and absurd analogies to dramatize existential points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of the military–industrial complex and profit-driven violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrays how modern economic motives generate violence independent of ideology—Milo Minderbinder's profiteering leads to morally ambiguous (even treacherous) acts presented without 'evil intent' but as greed-driven outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight systemic incentives and the normalization of profit over morality; present profiteers as rational within a corrupt logic to emphasize irony and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anachronism to situate critique beyond historical setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Although set in WWII, Heller intentionally includes anachronisms (e.g., loyalty oaths, IBM machines) to situate the novel in the context of the 1950s and to broaden the satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce anachronistic elements intentionally to draw parallels between the story's period and contemporary issues; don't mistake them for errors—their incongruity is a rhetorical device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing comic cushioning with an eventual dark/horrific reveal (tragicomedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For most of the book, the reader is cushioned from the full horror of war (implied by trauma); in the final sections the horrors are laid bare, producing a shift from comic farce to darker tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure tone so early humor builds reader investment and then allow a tonal shift to reveal underlying brutality; this contrast amplifies both comic and tragic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motif of bureaucratic absurdity and specious legalistic justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring motif is bureaucratic absurdity: the combination of force with specious and spurious legalistic justification (e.g., claims that Catch-22 exists and therefore cannot be repealed; agents need not prove provisions they enforce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create rules and rationales that sound legalistic or procedural but are internally inconsistent; present enforcement as self-justifying to expose institutional injustice comically and critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of words, phrases, and questions for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific words, phrases, and questions are repeated frequently to comic effect, often completing or echoing earlier jokes and creating a sense of déjà vu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select memorable lines or motifs and reuse them strategically to build running gags and thematic resonance across the narrative; repetition should accumulate meaning rather than be merely repetitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and numerical motifs as conceptual devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The title 'Catch-22' itself is a conceptual device; variations in the proposed titles (Catch-18, Catch-11, etc.) and the doubled digit relate to thematic ideas like déjà vu and repetition in the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider titular and numerical symbolism as part of the novel's rhetorical strategy; a striking title can encapsulate central paradoxes and sustain motif-driven humor.
